name: William P. Hobby Airport
before:
Houston's other airport, about 7 miles from the city centre, and the older of the two. It was the city's main airport until Intercontinental opened in 1969, closed briefly, then came back as the domestic and corporate airport.

Southwest runs it in practice. This is the airline's fifth largest station and it carries the vast majority of passengers here. Southwest built its first ever international terminal at Hobby, opening the West Concourse in October 2015 for flights to Mexico, Central America and South America.

There are 30 gates in one terminal across two concourses, 25 in the Central Concourse and five in the West. A 250 million dollar expansion announced in 2022 adds another seven.

Hobby became the first five star airport in North America under the Skytrax ratings in 2022, and in February 2020 the first in Texas with full biometric entry and exit for international passengers.

The original art deco terminal, the first passenger airline terminal in Houston, still stands and now houses the 1940 Air Terminal Museum.
after:
Houston's other airport, south east of downtown and the older of the two. It was the city's main airport until Intercontinental opened in 1969.

Southwest runs it in practice, carrying the vast majority of the airport's 13.9 million passengers in 2025. The airline built the West Concourse, which opened in October 2015 and brought back international flights, now to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

There are 30 gates across two concourses. A 470 million dollar expansion will add seven more to the West Concourse; Houston Airports expects it to finish in 2027.

Hobby became the first five star airport in North America under the Skytrax ratings in 2022.

The original 1940 Art Deco terminal still stands, but the 1940 Air Terminal Museum inside it closed in 2026, and the Texas Historical Commission is now deciding whether to reopen it as a state historic site.

claims.claim: about 7 miles from the city centre
claims.wasBefore: about 7 miles from the city centre
claims.why: Fails the coordinates check: 15.5 km (9.7 miles) in a straight line from the centre of Houston, a ratio of 0.72. The FAA's master record gives 8 nautical miles (9.2 statute miles); the operator, Wikipedia and the Handbook of Texas say 7 miles. The sources disagree, so the figure is dropped and the direction (south east) kept.

claims.claim: closed briefly, then came back as the domestic and corporate airport
claims.wasBefore: closed briefly, then came back as the domestic and corporate airport
claims.why: The sources disagree on 'closed': the Handbook of Texas says Hobby was made a general aviation airport for private and corporate aircraft in 1969 and some domestic airlines were back by 1971 (Southwest's own list dates its Hobby service from 14 November 1971), while Wikipedia says it closed and reopened 'after several years', which also contradicts 'briefly'. Left out for length; the return by 1971 has two sources (Handbook, Southwest) and could go back in.
